Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Tandem repeats (TRs), consisting of consecutive repeated units of 1+bp, are highly polymorphic features found throughout the genome that have been shown to have widespread impacts on gene expression and other traits.
However, despite their prevalence, TRs are not included as features in polygenic prediction models, which typically focus on common single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
Here, we develop a framework to incorporate TRs into gene expression models, which consider variants in a cis-window around each gene to predict expression levels.

Simulation analyses demonstrate that including linear effects of TR copy number as features can result in substantially improved predictions, particularly when high impact causal TRs are poorly tagged by individual SNPs.

We applied our framework to train and evaluate SNP+TR expression prediction models in lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) using data from the Geuvadis cohort (n=359 European individuals) and compared these to SNP-only models.

Overall, across 2,553 genes for which models trained successfully, we observed that SNP+TR models give significantly improved performance for 78 genes and a mean gain in adjusted R-squared 0.0037 across all genes, with most gains replicating in the independent Gene-Tissue Expression Project (GTEx) cohort.
We additionally find that incorporating TRs results in simpler models and improves portability of models when testing on data for 89 Yoruban individuals from Geuvadis.
Finally, we extended our models to consider nonlinear effects of TR copy number on expression.

Under our nonlinear TR association testing, we identify 2,255 nonlinear significant genes not captured by linear association testing models, and identify exemplar genes, including PALD1, with highly polymorphic TRs for which incorporating their nonlinear effects results in substantially improved gene expression prediction.

Overall, these results demonstrate the utility of including TRs in expression prediction models and show promise that they will have similar impact across other models such as polygenic risk scores for complex traits.
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been instrumental in identifying genetic variants associated with complex traits.
However, GWAS cannot directly discern how genetic variants in associated regions mechanistically impact a trait.

Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) [1] [2] [3] [4] attempt to address this shortcoming by identifying individual genes with genetically predicted expression levels that are associated with a trait such as diseases.

text.text: Compared to GWAS, TWAS offers easier interpretability by focusing on genes rather than individual variants; has improved power due to reduced multiple testing burden; and has the potential to generate tissue-specific hypotheses 5 .

text.text: Mostly, these gene expression prediction models focus on common single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and small indels in a cis-window around the gene.

They have not typically considered the contribution of more complex variant types such as repeats and structural variants which have been shown in some cases to have large contributions to expression [7] [8] [9] [10] [11].

text.text: Tandem repeats (TRs), which consist of repeating units of 1 or more bp in tandem, comprise over 2 million distinct loci throughout the human genome 12, 13 .

text.text: Here, we evaluate incorporating TRs alongside SNPs into gene expression prediction models.

To this end we used genotyping and RNA sequencing data from the 1000 Genomes Project 21, 22 and Geuvadis 23 for 359 European individuals to generate gene expression prediction models for 12,605 genes in lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs).

text.text: We evaluate the improvement of model predictions with TRs compared to SNP-only models, perform replication analysis in LCL data available from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Project, and compare cross-ancestry portability of SNP-only vs.

Finally, we assess the contribution of nonlinear effects of TR copy number on expression and incorporate these effects into gene expression prediction models.
Our results demonstrate that the models that incorporate TRs in some cases result in dramatic prediction performance improvement as well as simplified and more portable models.

Overall, our study demonstrates the benefit of considering a range of variant types for gene expression prediction models and suggests incorporating TRs will also benefit related applications such as polygenic risk scores for complex traits and diseases.

text.text: For this, we train LASSO regression models including either single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) alone, or SNPs in combination with TRs.

text.text: Finally, we evaluated whether incorporating nonlinear effects of TRs could improve gene expression prediction models.
In addition to the SNP-only and SNP+TR linear models above, we tested a third set of models for each gene containing SNPs as well as both linear and quadratic TR features for each TR included.
As in our association testing models (Methods), the quadratic term is composed of the sum of squared allele lengths for the two alleles in each diploid individual.
Overall, incorporation of quadratic TR effects resulted in improved adjusted R-squared values for 737 genes compared to the SNP-only and SNP+TR models.

text.text: Taken together, our results show that although robust examples of nonlinear effects of TRs on expression exist, incorporation into expression prediction models, at least using available sample sizes, has minimal overall improvement on prediction performance for most genes (Discussion).
Here, we presented a framework for incorporating TRs into prediction models.

Benchmarking our framework on simulated data demonstrated that including TRs can result in substantial improvement in predictive performance over SNP-only models, particularly at genes for which TRs with high effect sizes on expression are in weak to moderate LD with nearby SNPs.

By applying this framework to gene expression for LCLs, we found that incorporating TRs results in simplified LASSO models with fewer non-zero coefficients, and provides especially large performance gains for a subset of 83 genes.

For many genes, inclusion of TRs resulted in models that were more portable across ancestries, even when the SNP+TR model showed only a modest improvement in predictive performance over SNP-only models in the training European cohort.
Finally, we identified tens of thousands of examples of nonlinear associations between TR copy number and expression, with 252 associations that could only be detected when applying nonlinear models.

We highlight several strong examples of nonlinear effects, including a C n repeat associated with PALD1, and show that incorporating the nonlinear effect resulted in an improved gene expression prediction model.
We hypothesize that the gains in performance, portability, and simplification of prediction models is due to the direct inclusion of additional causal variants as predictors.
Current polygenic scores including gene expression prediction models primarily rely on common SNPs.
In many cases, the variants included are not causal, but rather serve as LD proxies for other underlying causal variants.

As a result, they may achieve low performance in cases where causal variants are not well tagged, and performance degrades when predicting on individuals of other ancestries with different LD structures.
Recent studies have demonstrated a widespread impact of TR variation on gene expression variability 10, 28 .

text.text: Our results have important implications for the design of polygenic risk scores (PRSs), which assess an individual's disease risk or other complex trait values based on their genetic variants.

text.text: Overall, this suggests incorporating TRs into PRS will have similar gains to those observed here for gene expression prediction models.
Our study faced several limitations.
First, the Geuvadis dataset only had a sufficiently large sample size to train across individuals of European ancestry.
While inclusion of TRs resulted in improved portability for some genes, TRs often show population-specific allele ranges and frequencies, whose effects will not be captured by our models here.

Expanding to additional datasets such as the multi-ethnic study of atherosclerosis (MESA) dataset which contains 574 European samples and 224 African samples of monocyte tissue 35 may result in improved models for non-European samples in future studies.

text.text: Third, we only considered a single cell type (LCLs).

Still, we anticipate the overall trends observed here will generalize to other settings, and that expanding to more cell types and tissues will identify additional genes for which incorporating TRs provides a major improvement in performance of gene expression prediction models.
Finally, our models are based on a limited sample size (n=359 samples from Geuvadis).
This limits our ability to accurately model variants with low effect sizes and contributes to high variance in expression predictions.
We also anticipate that low sample size reduces our ability to detect and model nonlinear effects.

Despite evidence from our recent work on massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA) 28 that nonlinear effects of TRs on expression may be widespread, we found only modest improvement in model performance when including nonlinear TR features.
text.formatted: Despite evidence from our recent work on massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">28</ref> that nonlinear effects of TRs on expression may be widespread, we found only modest improvement in model performance when including nonlinear TR features.

text.text: One potential explanation is that our use of a LASSO model with quadratic TR length effects is insufficient to capture some types of nonlinear trends.
Other model classes such as random forests, gradient boosting, or neural networks may better capture more complex relationships between TR length and expression.
However, these models are more expensive to train and require larger sample sizes to avoid overfitting.
Another challenge in modeling nonlinear effects at low sample sizes is that we may not observe a sufficient number of different TR lengths to reliably infer nonlinear trends.

For example, although we observed nonlinear trends when considering more than a dozen different repeat lengths at particular locus in an MPRA context 28 , if only two or three alleles are observed they may still be best fit by a linear model.

text.text: Overall, our results demonstrate that incorporating TRs into polygenic prediction models can result in improved and simpler models with improved portability across ancestries.

These results suggest that including additional potential sources of causal genetic variation beyond common SNPs in PRS and related methods is likely to result in improved prediction models for a range of traits.

We trained models to predict expression for each gene based on cis-variants using LASSO regression implemented in the scikit-learn package version 1.7.2 (ULRs) with non-default parameter max_iterations=50000 and tolerance 1e-4.
For each gene, we considered SNPs and TRs from an interval encompassing the gene boundaries +/-500kb.
Prior to training genotypes each variant was standardized to have mean zero and variance 1.
We trained two separate models for each gene, including either SNPs only or SNPs+TRs.
For each model, the alpha parameter for LASSO was tuned using the GridSearchCV class from scikit-learn to train models using 3-fold cross validation with n_repeats=2.
Tuning was performed in two steps, the first performed a broad search using a range of 0.1-0.9 with step 0.04.
The second performed a higher 18 resolution search using the value learned in the first round +/-0.09, with minimum allowable alpha 0.001, searching 51 possible values.
Due to our relatively low sample size (n=359 European samples), we repeated the training process above 20 times to assess variability in performance across runs.
For each gene we summarized the average R-squared, adjusted R-squared, and standard deviation across the 20 iterations.

text.text: We filtered TR loci with two or fewer unique alleles and with a heterozygosity less than 0.10.
To evaluate the gene expression model framework described below, we generated simulated gene expression values to assess whether incorporating TRs would improve model prediction accuracy.
In each case, we first identified causal SNPs and/or TRs within a 500kb window around a given gene and assigned each causal variant (SNP or TR) an effect size.
Simulations are based on real genotype data for the 359 European samples in the Geuvadis cohort to ensure they recapitulate realistic LD patterns.
The genotypes were Z-normalized before being passed to use for gene expression simulation and prediction.
In order to calculate LD in the below analyses we used the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficients from numpy version 2.2.6.
We used gene expression prediction models trained in the EUR cohort to predict expression for individuals from the YRI cohort of Geuvadis based on SNP and TR genotypes.
As in the EUR analysis, genotypes were Z-normalized to have mean 0 variance 1.
We compared predicted expression values to observed expression values for each sample, adjusted for 9 PEER factors, sex, and the top 5 genotype PCs computed from YRI samples.
Prior to comparing to predicted values, adjusted expression values were normalized to have mean 0 and variance 1.
For each gene, we computed the Pearson r 2 between predicted and observed expression values.
We performed linear and nonlinear association testing for TRs against nearby genes within the Geuvadis and GTEx datasets described above.
In Geuvadis, we utilized the same covariates as described above and in GTEx we used sex, the top 5 PCs, and 11 PEER factors as covariates.

For linear models, for each TR-gene pair, considering TRs within 500kb of the boundaries of each gene, we fit models of the form , where gives the sum of the TR lengths (Z-normalized to have mean 0 and 𝑌 = β(𝑥 1 + 𝑥 2 ) + γ𝐶 + ϵ 𝑥 1 + 𝑥 2 variance 1) of the two alleles of each individual, and other variables are defined as above.
For nonlinear association testing, we fit the model (in this case TR lengths are 𝑌 = β 𝑙 (𝑥 1 + 𝑥 2 ) + β 𝑛𝑙 (𝑥 1 2 + 𝑥 2 2 ) + γ𝐶 + ϵ not normalized).

This model assumes additive contributions to expression from the two chromosome copies, with each following a model , where is the expression coming from a single chromosome 𝑌' = β 𝑙 𝑥 + β 𝑛𝑙 𝑥 2 𝑌' copy and is the number of repeats on that same chromosome copy.
We computed P-values for each 𝑥 regression coefficient ( for linear models, and for nonlinear models) using the OLS function from β β 𝑙 β 𝑛𝑙 statsmodels version 0.14.6.
We additionally performed an ANOVA test using statsmodels anova_lm python function to determine whether nonlinear models provide an improved fit for each gene.
To identify genome-wide significant signals for either the linear or quadratic, we first identified the TR with the top P-value for each gene.
These were adjusted for the number of tests using a Bonferroni correction.
Adjusted top P-values were then used as input to a Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction to identify associations that are significant at a gene-level FDR of 5%.
A similar procedure was applied to ANOVA p-values comparing linear vs. nonlinear models.
To incorporate nonlinear effects into gene expression models, we similarly included an additional term for each TR.
However, unlike in our nonlinear association testing above, we normalized the sum of 𝑥 1 2 + 𝑥 2 2 the squares of the TR alleles to have mean 0 variance 1.
Normalization of these values is necessary in order to ensure the regularization term learned throughout the LASSO training process is generalizable to all features.

In the Geuvadis EUR cohort, this TR does not show a significant linear association with expression (two-sided P=0.61), but shows a significant quadratic effect (quadratic term two-sided P=3.25e-5) and a significantly better fit for the quadratic vs. linear model (ANOVA P=0.0013). Similar trends were observed in GTEx (linear P=0.99; quadratic P=1.1e-5; ANOVA
